stances.claim: Donald Trump can be labeled the 'best-suited' Potus given over 700 lawsuits filed against him and/or his actions in various US courts since his Jan 20 2025 inauguration -- about 30 appealed to SCOTUS (per New York Times). The most crucial suits center on his massive crackdown against alleged undocumented/overstaying migrants, his tariff impositions, his cancellation of federal aid to education, and the consequences of the US war with Iran.

Despite widespread criticisms, Trump expressed confidence in winning at SCOTUS, banking on the supermajority of six conservative justices (three named by him in his first term). He was upset when SCOTUS in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (Feb 20 2026) struck down his tariffs on Canada/Mexico/China imports -- CJ John Roberts joined by conservatives Gorsuch and Barrett plus three liberals (Sotomayor/Kagan/Jackson). Roberts clarified that 'the President asserts extraordinary power to unilaterally impose tariffs ... he must identify clear congressional authorization to exercise it.'

Stung by his defeat, Trump vented his ire on his two appointees Gorsuch and Barrett, lamenting 'they sicken me because they're bad for our country.' Trump conveniently forgot the conservative supermajority had almost always voted unanimously in his favor -- two examples: (1) DHS v. DVD (June 23 2025) -- 6-3 reversed Massachusetts district court requiring 'meaningful opportunity' for noncitizens to contest removal + lifted deportation restrictions to homeland AND third countries 'that would accept them' (three dissenting liberals criticized as 'gross abuse of the Court's equitable discretion'); (2) Trump v. CASA, Inc. (June 27 2025) -- 6-3 rejected 'universal injunctions' against ending birthright citizenship, with Barrett writing for the majority emphasizing lack of historical precedent, and Sotomayor in dissent calling the decision 'patently unconstitutional' cutting into the 14th Amendment's 'All persons born or naturalized in the United States ... are citizens.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Trump-conveniently-forgot + two-case illustration of conservative-supermajority-pro-Trump pattern

stances.claim: With its recent decisions, SCOTUS appeared to be supportive of Trump's questionable ways -- never mind that the Potus is increasingly losing in public opinion polls. A 2026 Reuters survey showed 64% of Americans opposed his elimination of birthright citizenship (32% agreed, 4% abstained); a Pew Research survey found 60% disapproved his tariff expansions. More telling, however, is the declining confidence in SCOTUS -- a 2025 Reuters/Ipsos poll found 58% of Americans do not view SCOTUS as politically neutral, with only 20% expressing confidence in its impartiality.

Having served the bar and the bench for almost seven decades, CJP has tried to emulate the SCOTUS of old when it was a bastion of liberty, prosperity, and the rule of law -- CJP is 'totally disjointed' to see the present SCOTUS appearing to lose long-term public trust to 'let justice be done though the heavens may fall.'

Yet CJP still hopes against hope that SCOTUS would one day catch up with the sparkle of CJ John Marshall, Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes, Benjamin Cardozo, William Brennan, Hugo Black, Joseph Story, Louis Brandeis, Thurgood Marshall, and others. CJP may not agree with everything they wrote, but will always cherish the passion, scholarship, and independence with which they expressed themselves, whether for the majority or for the minority.

CJP still looks forward to the day when SCOTUS would rebound to its old glory, for what happens in 'the land of the free and the home of the brave' reverberates around the world. When both its elected leader and its highest tribunal are perceived as less than fair and trustworthy, the consequences ripple far beyond US borders -- governments recalibrate, investors reassess, and jurists look elsewhere for models. SCOTUS is expected to rule on more immigrant/birthright-citizenship cases by end-of-June. One question remains: Will SCOTUS sail fairly and independently, or will it sink in the whirlpool of history along with the Potus?

notable_anecdotes: The Potus-Scotus titular wordplay -- pairing the two acronyms in a 'sink or sail' question -- among CJP's most memorable column-titles, using English-acronym sonorant-rhyme to dramatize institutional-fate interdependence.
The 'best-suited' Potus wry-label -- referring to Trump's record 700+ lawsuits with 'suit' as legal-action pun -- a sharp opening that doubles as wordplay.

Trump's 'they sicken me because they're bad for our country' verbatim outburst against his own appointees Gorsuch and Barrett -- captured as evidence of Trump's loyalty-as-jurisprudential-criterion mindset.

CJ Roberts's 'the President asserts extraordinary power to unilaterally impose tariffs ... he must identify clear congressional authorization' verbatim -- a clean separation-of-powers articulation captured for its civics-textbook clarity.
Sotomayor's 'patently unconstitutional' dissent verbatim -- quoting the full 14th Amendment birthright-citizenship clause as a constitutional anchor against the CASA majority.
The CJP autobiographical disclosure 'HAVING SERVED THE BAR AND THE BENCH FOR ALMOST SEVEN DECADES' -- establishing standing-to-opine through nearly-70-years-of-legal-service biography.

The historical-greats roster (Marshall + Holmes + Cardozo + Brennan + Black + Story + Brandeis + Thurgood Marshall) -- one of CJP's most concentrated SCOTUS-pantheon catalogs, emphasizing the historical baseline against which the present court is being measured.

The 'I may not agree with everything they have written, but I will always cherish the passion, scholarship, and independence' framing -- among CJP's most explicit articulations of his cross-ideological-judicial-virtue valuation criteria.
The 'let justice be done though the heavens may fall' Latin-axiom adaptation (fiat justitia ruat caelum) -- captured as the principle the present SCOTUS appears to be losing public-trust on.
The 'sink in the whirlpool of history along with the Potus' closing -- among CJP's most vivid maritime-metaphor framings for Potus-Scotus joint-fate questioning.
The 'totally disjointed' register-flex -- CJP's unusual word-choice (vs. 'disheartened' or 'troubled') signaling pointed deliberate displeasure with the present SCOTUS.

The 'Governments recalibrate, investors reassess, and jurists look elsewhere for models' tripartite-consequence -- among CJP's tightest catalogs of the global-spillover effects of US-institutional-credibility decline.
